forces: Harp, flute, clarinet and string quartet
performers: Karen Grimsey, harp; Kara Santos, flute; Parker Gaims, clarinet; Sara Matayoshi and Foster Wang, violins; Tam Tran, viola; Clayton Vaughn, cello — United States Marine Band
intro: Ravel’s Introduction and Allegro is written for harp and six other players. Karen Grimsey plays the harp part with winds and strings from the United States Marine Band, and she plays the long cadenza alone.

sections.label: Intro · Flute and clarinet duet
sections.mNote: The strings join the flute and clarinet before the harp enters.

sections.label: A · Harp solo
sections.mNote: Allegro. A melody set within descending broken chords.

sections.label: Dev · Harp and ensemble alternate phrases
sections.mNote: Harp solo passages alternate with phrases for wind and strings

sections.label: Cadenza · Harp arpeggios, chords and harmonics
sections.mNote: The other six players rest; the harp plays alone.

sections.label: Intro · Winds and muted strings, soft
sections.mNote: The opening tempo returns with the harp.

sections.label: A′ · Clarinet theme over harp accompaniment
sections.mNote: The clarinet takes over the theme first played by the harp.

sections.label: Coda · Harp, winds and strings
sections.mNote: Harp glissandos with fast wind figures and pizzicato strings

cues.title: Opening duet, flute and clarinet
cues.text: Flute and clarinet open with a soft duet. Violin, viola and cello join them, and the harp then plays an upward run through their held notes. The second violin has not yet entered.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1906), p. 3, opening four bars. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IMSLP06186-Ravel_-_Introduction_et_Allegro,_score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Commission from Érard, 1905
cues.text: In 1905 Érard commissioned Ravel to show what its pedal harp could do. The rival firm Pleyel had already commissioned Debussy’s Danses for its chromatic harp. Ravel set the harp among flute, clarinet and four strings.
cues.evidence: Jane Vial Jaffe, programme note on the commissions from Pleyel and Érard: https://www.parlancechamberconcerts.org/individual-program-notes/maurice-ravel-%281875-1937%29/introduction-and-allegro.

cues.title: Allegro, harp melody
cues.text: At the Allegro the harp plays nearly alone. Its melody lies at the top of descending broken chords, marked le chant en dehors. Low harmonics sound beneath the quick notes.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, p. 8, rehearsal 2: Allegro, le chant en dehors and harp harmonics beneath the melody.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Manuscript left at a shirt shop, 1905
cues.text: In 1905 Ravel hurried to finish the score before a holiday aboard Alfred and Misia Edwards’s yacht. He left the manuscript at a shirt shop, missed the boat and had to persuade the music-loving shopkeeper to return it. He joined the yacht at Soissons.
cues.evidence: The manuscript, chemisier and missed departure are recounted by Jane Vial Jaffe: https://www.parlancechamberconcerts.org/individual-program-notes/maurice-ravel-%281875-1937%29/introduction-and-allegro.

cues.title: Harp cadenza
cues.text: The harp plays a cadenza. Arpeggios climb from the bass and are interrupted by slow chords, and glissandos lead into harmonics. Karen Grimsey plays the melody, the bass and the resonance alone.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 26–27: Cadenza, rubato, Lent, Très lent, glissandos and harmonics.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the introduction’s tempo
cues.text: At rehearsal 18 Ravel restores the tempo of the introduction (1° Tempo). Flute and clarinet return at ppp, with muted strings around the harp. The cello plays pizzicato.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, p. 27, rehearsal 18: 1° Tempo, ppp winds, muted strings and pizzicato cello.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Clarinet melody over harp, rehearsal 20
cues.text: The harp’s Allegro figures return, and the clarinet now plays the tune above them. Flute and strings rest.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, p. 29, rehearsal 20: solo clarinet above harp figuration; flute and strings rest.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing bars in G♭ major
cues.text: The harp plays its final glissandos while the string quartet plays pizzicato. Flute and clarinet play short attacks. All seven players end on a G♭-major chord.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, p. 39: final harp glissandos, pizzicato strings, wind attacks and G♭-major close.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Harp alone at the Allegro
transitions.how: At the Allegro (rehearsal 2), the winds and strings release their held notes and the harp begins its descending broken chords. Ravel marks the tune le chant en dehors. Harmonics sustain the bass beneath it, and the other six instruments stop playing.

transitions.title: Harp cadenza over held ensemble chord
transitions.from: Dev · Harp and ensemble alternate phrases
transitions.to: Cadenza · Harp arpeggios, chords and harmonics
transitions.how: The ensemble holds a chord while the harp begins low arpeggios, marked Cadenza and rubato. The winds and strings release the chord, and the arpeggios rise into the upper register. Slower chords and harmonics follow, marked Lent and Très lent.

transitions.title: Muted strings around the harp
transitions.from: Cadenza · Harp arpeggios, chords and harmonics
transitions.to: Intro · Winds and muted strings, soft
transitions.how: The harp’s harmonics lead into 1° Tempo. Flute and clarinet return at ppp, the bowed strings put on mutes and the cello plays a pizzicato bass. The harp continues beneath the sustained phrases of the opening.

transitions.title: Clarinet takes over the harp’s tune
transitions.from: Intro · Winds and muted strings, soft
transitions.to: A′ · Clarinet theme over harp accompaniment
transitions.how: The ensemble releases its chord and the harp resumes its Allegro arpeggios. At rehearsal 20 the clarinet enters softly with the melody, above the harp’s running figures and low harmonics. Flute and strings rest, leaving a duet for clarinet and harp.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 28–29, Allegro and rehearsal 20.

source.title: Ravel, Introduction et Allegro — original seven-player full score, Durand, 1906
source.locator: Opening and rehearsals 2, 4, 18 and 20; printed pp. 3, 8, 11, 26–30 and 39. One player takes each of the seven parts.

timeline.note: Flute and clarinet begin alone, in a soft duet.
First violin, viola and cello join the winds before the harp moves upwards. The second violin is silent.
All seven players join in the closing phrases of the introduction before the harp begins the Allegro alone.
The harp begins the Allegro with a melody set within descending broken chords. The ensemble releases its held chord.
The flute plays above the harp’s arpeggios and harmonics. The violins move in quick notes; the cello plays its bass line pizzicato.
The harp plays the cadenza alone, rising through arpeggios before slower chords and harmonics.
Flute and clarinet return softly, with muted strings and harp. The cello plays pizzicato.
The harp’s Allegro figures return, then the clarinet enters with the melody above them.
Flute and strings rejoin the clarinet and harp. The wind phrases rise over the harp’s continuing arpeggios.

composer.epithet: Composer of a ballet built from two tunes and a snare drum, and of a suite of dances dedicated to his war dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery, and his mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He went back to the Basque coast many times. Spain appears often in his music, in the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera in the Rapsodie espagnole and the clocks of a Toledo clockmaker’s shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. André Gedalge gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and in January 1898 he entered the composition class of Fauré. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces he could not have played himself with comparable command.
